name: house-style description: The house frontend conventions for this repo, layered on top of the SpartanNG docs. Read before writing or editing any component. Covers BEM markup with Tailwind applied in the component stylesheet, the three-file component, the layout grammar (grid for regions, flex for inline runs, no nested flex faking a grid) and the no-raw-literals rule for hand-written CSS. Where these rules and the spartan docs' examples disagree about where utility classes go, these rules win. --- # House frontend conventions These are this repo's conventions, layered on top of the SpartanNG docs (the `spartan` skill). They extend the spartan docs where spartan is silent; they never contradict them. Where spartan already has a rule (semantic colors, `class` is for layout only, `gap-*` not `space-*`, `size-*` for equal dimensions), follow the spartan skill; this file adds only what spartan does not cover. One deliberate exception: spartan's examples put Tailwind utilities in the template's `class` attribute. In this repo they never go there; see "Markup is BEM, styling lives in the stylesheet" below. Every other spartan rule stands, including "class is for layout only" on a primitive, which now means the utilities a primitive's BEM class applies must be layout only. ## Markup is BEM, styling lives in the stylesheet A template says what things are; the stylesheet says how they look. Utility classes in markup turn every template into a wall of `flex items-center gap-3 sm:w-48` that a reader has to decode to find the structure, and they let styling decisions spread across every file that renders the element. So: 1. **Template classes are BEM names only.** Every token in a `class` attribute, every `[class.x]` binding, and every string inside a `[class]` binding is `block`, `block__element`, `block--modifier` or `block__element--modifier`, lowercase kebab-case. No Tailwind utility appears in a template. That includes `sr-only`: write `class="roster__label"` and `@apply sr-only` it. 2. **One block per component, named after the component file.** `hero-card.ts` owns `.hero-card`, `.hero-card__name`, `.hero-card--retired`, and nothing else. A template must not use another component's block, and a stylesheet must not define one. `:host` is allowed. 3. **Every component is three files.** `hero-card.ts` with `templateUrl: './hero-card.html'` and `styleUrl: './hero-card.css'`. Never `template:` or `styles:`, however small the component. `ng g component` already produces this shape. 4. **Stylesheets are plain `.css` with every BEM class written out in full.** Not `.scss`: Tailwind v4 does not support running behind Sass. The first line is always `@reference "../../styles.css";` (adjust the `../` count to the file's depth under `src/app`), which lets `@apply` resolve the theme's tokens and variants. Write `.roster__row { ... }`, never `.roster { &__row { ... } }`: that is Sass syntax, and native CSS compiles it to a selector that matches nothing, with only a warning. Nesting is fine for states and breakpoints on the same element: `&:hover`, `&::before`, `&[aria-expanded="true"]`, `@media`. 5. **Utilities live in `@apply`, and every rule below still applies to them.** Semantic color tokens only, `gap-*` not `space-*`, grid for regions, appearance never on a primitive. Moving a utility from the template into `@apply` does not change whether it is allowed. 6. **No utility classes in TypeScript.** No `cva` variant strings, no `host: { class: '...' }`, no computed class strings. A state that changes appearance is a BEM modifier bound with `[class.block--modifier]`. Never build a class name from data (`roster__row--{{ hero.status }}`): write one modifier per state and bind each with `[class.roster__row--active]`, so every class a template can carry is written out in full. Helm directives and their inputs are not classes and stay in the template: `variant`, `size` and the directive itself are the primitive's API. ```html

Roster

Recruit
@for (hero of vm.heroes(); track hero.id) {
{{ hero.name }}
}
``` ```css /* roster.css */ @reference "../../styles.css"; .roster { @apply grid gap-6; } .roster__title { @apply text-2xl font-semibold; } .roster__filters { @apply flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3; } .roster__label { @apply sr-only; } .roster__search { @apply w-full sm:w-64; } .roster__recruit { @apply ms-auto; } .roster__row { @apply text-sm; &:hover { @apply bg-accent; } } .roster__row--retired { @apply text-muted-foreground; } ``` Note the primitives: `roster__search` and `roster__recruit` apply only width and margin, because a primitive's class is for layout only. Color, typography, border, radius, shadow and internal padding for a primitive come from its own `variant`/`size` inputs, never from the app's stylesheet, and moving them into `@apply` behind a BEM name does not make them allowed. When no existing variant gives the look you need (an input padded to make room for an icon, a quieter table cell, a rounded panel), add a variant to the primitive itself: edit the owned copy of its component in `libs/ui`, add the variant to its `cva` using semantic tokens only, and select it from the template with the input (``). `libs/ui` is the one place `cva` and utility strings in TypeScript belong; rule 6 applies to `src/app`. One variant serves every screen that needs the look, which is the point: a primitive's appearance is decided in one place, not re-decided at every call site. ## The sealed control vocabulary Helm primitives are copied into `libs/ui`, so the set of primitives this repo owns is exactly what that directory ships. Where a primitive covers a native element, use the primitive. Reaching for the bare native element is the drift this rule exists to stop, and it is the one convention worth reading before writing any template. Most primitives are directives you put on the native element, so the markup stays native and accessible and only picks up the Helm styling and behavior. A few have no directive twin and replace the native element outright. Read before writing or editing any component. Covers BEM markup with Tailwind applied in the component stylesheet, the three-file component, the layout grammar (grid for regions, flex for inline runs, no nested flex faking a grid) and the no-raw-literals rule for hand-written CSS. Where these rules and the spartan docs' examples disagree about where utility classes go, these rules win. --- # House frontend conventions These are this repo's conventions, layered on top of the SpartanNG docs (the `spartan` skill). They extend the spartan docs where spartan is silent; they never contradict them. Where spartan already has a rule (semantic colors, `class` is for layout only, `gap-*` not `space-*`, `size-*` for equal dimensions), follow the spartan skill; this file adds only what spartan does not cover. One deliberate exception: spartan's examples put Tailwind utilities in the template's `class` attribute. In this repo they never go there; see "Markup is BEM, styling lives in the stylesheet" below. Every other spartan rule stands, including "class is for layout only" on a primitive, which now means the utilities a primitive's BEM class applies must be layout only. ## Markup is BEM, styling lives in the stylesheet A template says what things are; the stylesheet says how they look. Utility classes in markup turn every template into a wall of `flex items-center gap-3 sm:w-48` that a reader has to decode to find the structure, and they let styling decisions spread across every file that renders the element. So: 1. **Template classes are BEM names only.** Every token in a `class` attribute, every `[class.x]` binding, and every string inside a `[class]` binding is `block`, `block__element`, `block--modifier` or `block__element--modifier`, lowercase kebab-case. No Tailwind utility appears in a template. That includes `sr-only`: write `class="roster__label"` and `@apply sr-only` it. 2. **One block per component, named after the component file.** `hero-card.ts` owns `.hero-card`, `.hero-card__name`, `.hero-card--retired`, and nothing else. A template must not use another component's block, and a stylesheet must not define one. `:host` is allowed. 3. **Every component is three files.** `hero-card.ts` with `templateUrl: './hero-card.html'` and `styleUrl: './hero-card.css'`. Never `template:` or `styles:`, however small the component. `ng g component` already produces this shape. 4. **Stylesheets are plain `.css` with every BEM class written out in full.** Not `.scss`: Tailwind v4 does not support running behind Sass. The first line is always `@reference "../../styles.css";` (adjust the `../` count to the file's depth under `src/app`), which lets `@apply` resolve the theme's tokens and variants. Write `.roster__row { ... }`, never `.roster { &__row { ... } }`: that is Sass syntax, and native CSS compiles it to a selector that matches nothing, with only a warning. Nesting is fine for states and breakpoints on the same element: `&:hover`, `&::before`, `&[aria-expanded="true"]`, `@media`. 5. **Utilities live in `@apply`, and every rule below still applies to them.** Semantic color tokens only, `gap-*` not `space-*`, grid for regions, appearance never on a primitive. Moving a utility from the template into `@apply` does not change whether it is allowed. 6. **No utility classes in TypeScript.** No `cva` variant strings, no `host: { class: '...' }`, no computed class strings. A state that changes appearance is a BEM modifier bound with `[class.block--modifier]`. Never build a class name from data (`roster__row--{{ hero.status }}`): write one modifier per state and bind each with `[class.roster__row--active]`, so every class a template can carry is written out in full. - Use signals for local component state

## Templates

- Keep templates simple and avoid complex logic
